body:
The rise of the Chalukyas in the Deccan

The Chalukyas of Badami, also called the Early Chalukyas or Chalukyas of Vatapi, were an important ruling dynasty of the western Deccan from the 6th to the mid-8th century CE. Their political centre lay in present-day Karnataka, and their power extended over substantial parts of peninsular India.

The Deccan is the plateau region of peninsular India. The Chalukyan kingdom developed around important river valleys, particularly the Krishna, Tungabhadra and Malaprabha. The region between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers is known as the Raichur Doab. The term doab means land between 2 rivers.

The Chalukyas were prominent contemporaries of the Pallavas of Kanchipuram. Their rivalry shaped the political history of southern India during the 7th century.

The founding of the kingdom

Pulakeshin I consolidated Chalukya power around 543 CE by establishing control over the area surrounding Badami. The town was also known as Vatapi and developed into the dynasty's principal royal capital.

The best-known ruler was Pulakeshin II, whose reign is generally dated to approximately 610–642 CE. He expanded Chalukya influence and successfully resisted the southward advance of Harshavardhana.

The dynasty continued after Pulakeshin II. Its later rulers included Vikramaditya II, during whose reign important temples were constructed at Pattadakal. By the middle of the 8th century, the Rashtrakutas had displaced the Early Chalukyas as the dominant power in the region.

Three important Chalukyan centres

The history of this dynasty is closely associated with 3 places in present-day Karnataka.

  • Aihole: An early Chalukyan centre and an important place for experimentation in temple construction. It is also associated with the famous inscription of Pulakeshin II.
  • Badami or Vatapi: The principal royal capital, especially known for its rock-cut cave temples and structural temples.
  • Pattadakal: A ceremonial centre associated with royal coronations and celebrated for its large stone temples.

Aihole is also described as an early capital in historical accounts. Therefore, the important distinction is between Aihole's early political and religious significance and Badami's position as the principal capital from which the dynasty takes its conventional name.

Historical and architectural importance

The Chalukyas are remembered for both their political achievements and their contribution to Indian temple architecture. Their builders constructed rock-cut temples, excavated from existing rock, as well as structural temples, assembled from individual stone blocks.

Early Chalukyan architecture developed through experimentation with different temple plans and towers. This development is particularly visible at Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal.

Prelims focus

  • Early Chalukyas: approximately 6th to mid-8th century CE.
  • Pulakeshin I established control around Badami in approximately 543 CE.
  • Pulakeshin II ruled approximately 610–642 CE.
  • Badami was also called Vatapi and served as the principal capital.
  • Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal are in present-day Karnataka.
  • Trap: Do not confuse the Badami Chalukyas with the later Chalukyas or Chaulukyas associated with Gujarat.

[NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts–I, Chapter 11, New Empires and Kingdoms, pp. 115–116; NCERT, Class 11, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, pp. 85–87; Archaeological Survey of India, Dharwad Circle, The Group of Monuments, sections Historical Perspective and Architectural Achievements, consulted 18 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Evolution of Temple Architecture – Aihole-Badami-Pattadakal, Tentative List submission dated 9 February 2015, Description, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: Where the Badami Chalukyas Ruled and When

body:
Pulakeshin II and the expansion of Chalukya power

Pulakeshin II was the most prominent ruler of the Early Chalukya dynasty. He ruled from Badami, or Vatapi, during approximately 610–642 CE.

His reign brought the Chalukyas into direct conflict with powerful rulers to the north and south. His military expeditions also extended towards the western and eastern coastal regions of peninsular India.

How Pulakeshin II checked Harshavardhana

Harshavardhana, commonly called Harsha, ruled much of northern India during the first half of the 7th century. He was associated with Thanesar and subsequently Kannauj.

After establishing his power in northern India, Harsha attempted to extend his influence southward into the Deccan. His advance was checked by Pulakeshin II near the Narmada River.

This event is important because it demonstrated that Harsha's military power did not extend successfully into the western Deccan. The Narmada became an important geographical marker between the northern sphere of Harsha and the Chalukyan sphere of power to the south.

Pulakeshin II checked Harshavardhana's southward advance at the Narmada. Harsha was the northern ruler whose expansion was stopped; Pulakeshin II was the Chalukyan ruler responsible for stopping it.

The conflict with the Pallavas

Another important rival of Pulakeshin II was the Pallava dynasty, whose capital was Kanchipuram in present-day Tamil Nadu.

The Chalukyas and Pallavas frequently fought over territory and political influence in southern India. Their conflicts also involved attacks on prosperous royal centres.

Pulakeshin II fought against the Pallava ruler Mahendravarman I. The Chalukyan account describes a campaign in which the Pallava ruler withdrew behind the defensive walls of Kanchipuram.

The conflict, however, did not end with a permanent Chalukyan victory. The Pallava ruler Narasimhavarman I, also known as Mamalla, subsequently defeated the Chalukyas and captured Vatapi around 642 CE.

This provides an important chronological distinction. Pulakeshin II achieved successes against the Pallavas, but the Pallavas later retaliated successfully. A victory during one phase of the rivalry should not be mistaken for permanent control of the opposing kingdom.

Military events and their outcomes

Ruler or dynastyRelationship with Pulakeshin IIImportant result
HarshavardhanaNorthern rivalHis southward advance was checked near the Narmada.
Mahendravarman IPallava opponentPulakeshin II campaigned against the Pallavas of Kanchipuram.
Narasimhavarman ILater Pallava opponentCaptured Vatapi around 642 CE.

Why the distinction matters

Harsha and the Pallavas were separate opponents of Pulakeshin II. Harsha ruled in northern India and attempted to advance into the Deccan. The Pallavas ruled from Kanchipuram and competed directly with the Chalukyas for influence in southern India.

Historical accounts of the period therefore contain both a major northern success for Pulakeshin II and a later southern reversal for the Chalukyas.

Prelims focus

  • Pulakeshin II: approximately 610–642 CE.
  • Harshavardhana's southward advance was checked near the Narmada.
  • The Pallavas ruled from Kanchipuram.
  • Mahendravarman I was a Pallava opponent of Pulakeshin II.
  • Narasimhavarman I, also called Mamalla, captured Vatapi around 642 CE.
  • Trap: The Chalukyan success against Mahendravarman I and the later Pallava capture of Vatapi occurred in different phases of the conflict.

[NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts–I, Chapter 11, New Empires and Kingdoms, pp. 115–116; NCERT, Class 11, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, p. 84; Government of Karnataka, Bagalkote District Administration, Badami Caves, historical introduction, consulted 18 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, Epigraphia Indica, Volume VI, F. Kielhorn, Aihole Inscription of Pulakesin II, pp. 1–12, consulted online 18 November 2026.]

title: Pulakeshin II: Harsha, the Pallavas and the Deccan

body:
What is the Aihole inscription?

The Aihole inscription is one of the most important historical records associated with Pulakeshin II of the Badami Chalukya dynasty. It records the ruler's achievements and provides information about his military campaigns.

The inscription is located on the wall of the Meguti Jain Temple at Aihole in present-day Karnataka.

It was composed in Sanskrit by Ravikirti, a poet associated with the court of Pulakeshin II.

The inscription is dated to Shaka year 556, corresponding to approximately 634–635 CE. This is a date associated with the inscription, not the beginning of Pulakeshin II's reign.

What is a prashasti?

A prashasti is a composition praising a ruler or another important person. Royal prashastis commonly describe victories, achievements, titles and qualities of the ruler.

The Aihole inscription is a royal prashasti. Ravikirti composed it to celebrate Pulakeshin II and his accomplishments.

Because a prashasti is written in praise of its subject, its descriptions of victories and personal qualities must be understood as claims made by the author. Its importance lies in the historical information it preserves, including identifiable people, places, events and dates.

What does Ravikirti record?

The inscription describes several achievements attributed to Pulakeshin II.

  • Conflict with Harsha: It celebrates the checking of Harshavardhana's advance towards the Deccan.
  • Coastal expeditions: It describes campaigns extending towards the western and eastern coastal regions.
  • Conflict with the Pallavas: It records a campaign against the Pallavas of Kanchipuram.
  • Royal reputation: It praises Pulakeshin II as a powerful and successful ruler.

The record also connects Ravikirti with the construction of the Jain temple in which the inscription was placed. Thus, the inscription is associated with both the political history of the Chalukyas and the religious architecture of Aihole.

The inscription's date and historical setting

The Shaka era is a chronological system whose conventional starting point is 78 CE. In the ordinary conversion of completed Shaka years, the addition of 78 gives the corresponding CE year.

For the Aihole record, Shaka year 556 is conventionally expressed as 634–635 CE. The range reflects the historical dating of the completed era year rather than uncertainty about which ruler the inscription praises.

The important relationship is that the inscription was created during the reign of Pulakeshin II and records achievements already attributed to him by that time.

Distinguishing the Aihole inscription from Harsha's biography

The history of Pulakeshin II and Harsha is associated with 2 different literary works.

WorkAuthorAssociated ruler
Aihole inscriptionRavikirtiPulakeshin II
HarshacharitaBanabhattaHarshavardhana

Harshacharita is a Sanskrit biography of Harsha written by his court poet Banabhatta. The Aihole inscription, by contrast, is a Sanskrit royal praise inscription composed by Ravikirti in connection with Pulakeshin II.

Prelims focus

  • Aihole inscription: Pulakeshin II of the Badami Chalukyas.
  • Composer: Ravikirti.
  • Language: Sanskrit.
  • Date: Shaka 556, corresponding to 634–635 CE.
  • Location: Meguti Jain Temple, Aihole, Karnataka.
  • Harshacharita: Banabhatta's biography of Harshavardhana.
  • Trap: The Aihole inscription was composed by Ravikirti, not by Banabhatta or Pulakeshin II himself.

[Archaeological Survey of India, Epigraphia Indica, Volume VI, 1900–1901, F. Kielhorn, Aihole Inscription of Pulakesin II, pp. 1–12, particularly the discussion of the date and the inscription's contents; NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts–I, Chapter 11, New Empires and Kingdoms, pp. 114–116; Government of Karnataka, Bagalkote District Administration, Aihole, section Meguti Temple, consulted 18 November 2026.]

body:
Badami as a centre of temple architecture

Badami, historically known as Vatapi, was the principal capital of the Early Chalukyas. Besides its political importance, it became a major centre of religious architecture during the 6th and 7th centuries CE.

Badami is particularly famous for its 4 major rock-cut cave temples, excavated into the sandstone cliffs.

A rock-cut temple is created by removing stone from an existing rock mass to form spaces such as an entrance, hall, pillars and sanctuary. It differs from a structural temple, which is constructed by placing separate building materials together.

The 4 principal cave temples

The Badami caves illustrate the presence of different religious traditions in Early Chalukyan art.

Cave 1: Shaiva tradition

Cave 1 is mainly associated with Shiva. Its most recognisable sculpture depicts Shiva as Nataraja, the dancing form of Shiva.

The Nataraja sculpture at Badami has 18 arms, arranged to represent different dance movements. Other important carvings include Ardhanarishvara, representing Shiva and Parvati in a combined form.

The cave's association with Shiva makes it a clear example of Shaiva religious art.

Cave 2: Vaishnava tradition

Cave 2 is associated principally with Vishnu. Important sculptures include Trivikrama, the form of Vishnu associated with the 3 strides, and Varaha, the boar incarnation.

These images help identify Cave 2 as a major example of Vaishnava art.

Cave 3: A larger Vaishnava cave

Cave 3 is the largest of the 4 principal caves. It is predominantly associated with Vaishnava themes, although its sculpture also includes Shaiva imagery.

Important carvings include Vishnu as Trivikrama, Varaha and Narasimha, and Vishnu on Ananta. The last image depicts Vishnu seated on the coils of the serpent Ananta.

An inscription associated with this cave records its establishment in 578 CE in connection with Mangalesha, an early Chalukya prince who subsequently became ruler.

Cave 4: Jain tradition

Cave 4 belongs to the Jain tradition. It contains sculptures of Jain Tirthankaras, including Mahavira.

A Tirthankara is a revered spiritual teacher in Jainism who shows the path to liberation. The presence of a Jain cave alongside Hindu caves demonstrates the variety of religious monuments built in the Chalukyan region.

Structural temples at Badami

Badami was not limited to rock-cut temples. The region also contains structural stone temples associated with Early Chalukyan architectural development.

Important examples include the Bhutanatha Temple near the Agastya water tank and the Malegitti Shivalaya, which has a southern or Dravida-type temple tower.

The presence of rock-cut caves and separately built stone temples at Badami helps explain the transition towards more elaborate structural temple architecture.

Prelims focus

  • Badami is also known as Vatapi.
  • The main Badami cave group contains 4 caves.
  • Cave 1: Shaiva; famous for the 18-armed Nataraja.
  • Caves 2 and 3: predominantly Vaishnava.
  • Cave 3: the largest cave; associated with a 578 CE inscription.
  • Cave 4: Jain; contains an image of Mahavira.
  • Trap: Cave 4 is Jain, not another predominantly Vaishnava cave.

[Government of Karnataka, Bagalkote District Administration, Badami Caves, sections Cave I, Cave II, Cave III, Cave IV and Badami Fort, consulted 18 November 2026; NCERT, Class 11, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, pp. 85–87; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Evolution of Temple Architecture – Aihole-Badami-Pattadakal, Tentative List Description, section Group of Temples and Caves in Badami, consulted 18 November 2026.]
